t: How To Create An Independent, Motivated, And Mature Class
q: But there is danger lurking. You see, at the first sign of peace, it’s all too common to start believing the lie that you’re not doing enough.
They assist and handhold and coddle, all the while undermining a critical part of the learning process and removing what students crave—and need—most: Freedom and responsibility.
This causes boredom, irritability, low motivation, and the desire for you to personally reteach individually what you taught the entire class just minutes before.
But once these are established, you must cut your students loose. Really cut them loose. Send the message that independent work, whether individual or in groups, is truly independent.
Shift 100% of the responsibility for doing the work over to your class while you fade into a corner to observe and take in the big picture.
Take more of you out of the picture, and you’ll discover your students becoming staggeringly more mature, independent, and responsible.

t: A Mysterious But Powerful Way To Improve Listening istening/
q: But what we have yet to cover is perhaps the single most important key to improving listening.
In fact, why it works so well is a bit of a mystery. Because, you see, it’s not about what you do. It’s about what you believe.
It comes from doing what you say you’re going to do. It comes from your consistency and follow through.
For every time you go back on your word or let misbehavior go without the consequence you promised, you weaken your influence and lose trust in the eyes of your students.
There is an unmistakable aura that accompanies teachers with authentic conviction, a distinct vibration of speech that is borne of the perfect symmetry between words and actions.
Do what you say and when you say you’re going to do it, and you’ll speak with a mysterious power that can move mountains.
x: Michael Linsin moves past mechanical listening tips like volume, pacing, and eye contact to argue that the single most important factor in whether students listen is conviction — the felt belief behind a teacher's words.

t: A (Slightly) Dangerous But Effective Way To Get Your Students' Attention
q: Okay, so I’ve got this strategy I’ve been using a long time. But I’ve been reluctant to share it. Because, you see, it can, potentially anyway, be an eensy-weensy bit dangerous.
But if you add this one little (slightly) dangerous part to it, and don’t use it too often, you can bring an extra layer of urgency to your message.
There is something about the added height—the novelty or whimsicalness of it—that causes students to understand innately that you have something important to tell them.

Now, it’s important to reiterate that you should never jump up on just any chair in the spur of the moment. Check beforehand to make sure that the one you choose is stable, sturdy, reliable, can hold your weight, etc.
I feel comfortable using the strategy and always have. But please, if you decide to try it, be careful. I'd be horrified if videos of teachers losing their balance started popping up on YouTube.
It probably goes without saying, but it’s a good idea to remind your students that the strategy is a teaching tool only, and they may not repeat the practice.

t: How To Handle A Student Who Questions You With Disrespect
q: The "question" usually comes out of left field, catching you off guard. It's almost always public, confrontational, and in the form of a challenge.
It’s best not to respond to their question—at least not right away. Instead, defuse the tension in the room by deferring your answer to a later time.
Wait at least twenty minutes before approaching the student. This way, you give them a chance to calm down and rethink the manner in which they posed their question.
Avoid pulling the student aside for a private chat or otherwise making the situation bigger and more important than it is.
However, it's important to note that the incident itself is a sign that you're not adequately explaining the why of what you do.

Because when your students know why they must work silently or raise their hand or rewrite essays, or follow any other rule, policy, or procedure . . . They’re far more willing, and even eager, to go along with it.
x: Michael Linsin offers a three-step strategy for handling students who challenge a teacher's authority in the guise of a disrespectful public question.
Deferring the response in the moment ('now's not a good time... we can talk') avoids giving the student a public forum and prevents the situation from escalating.
Waiting about twenty minutes lets tension subside and shifts control of the situation back to the teacher.
